sections.h: Death, joy and the poor wise man (Ecclesiastes 9)
sections.b: Chapter 9 faces death head-on. The righteous and the wise are in God's hand, but "one fate comes to everyone" (Ecclesiastes 9:3), and "the dead do not know a thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5). From that fact comes the book's strongest call to joy: eat your bread in joy, wear white, see life with the woman you love, and do what you can with your strength, "for there is no doing and no reckoning, no knowledge and no wisdom in Sheol" (Ecclesiastes 9:7–10). Time and chance meet everyone (Ecclesiastes 9:11), and a poor wise man who saved his town is forgotten (Ecclesiastes 9:13–16).

Chapter 10 is the book's most Proverbs-like chapter. "Dead flies turn a perfumer's oil foul and frothy" (Ecclesiastes 10:1): a little folly outweighs wisdom. Qohelet sees slaves on horses and princes on foot (Ecclesiastes 10:7), warns that every task has its risk (Ecclesiastes 10:8–11), mocks the fool's many words (Ecclesiastes 10:12–15) and ends with sayings about kings, including the warning that "a bird of the sky will carry off the sound" (Ecclesiastes 10:20).

sections.h: Cast your bread, and the final poem (Ecclesiastes 11–12)
sections.b: Chapter 11 turns uncertainty into action: "Send your bread out over the surface of the water" (Ecclesiastes 11:1), and "Whoever keeps an eye on the wind will not sow" (Ecclesiastes 11:4). Then the final poem speaks to a young man: be glad in your youth, but "for all of it God will bring you into judgment" (Ecclesiastes 11:9). "Remember your Creator in the days of your prime" (Ecclesiastes 12:1) opens the Bible's great picture of old age and death, which ends as "the spirit goes back to God, who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7). Qohelet's last words repeat his first: "Everything is vapor" (Ecclesiastes 12:8).

The frame narrator speaks about Qohelet: he was wise, taught the people, "put many proverbs in order" and wrote "words of truth" (Ecclesiastes 12:9–10). "The words of the wise are like ox goads" (Ecclesiastes 12:11), but "making many books has no end" (Ecclesiastes 12:12). The book ends: "Fear God and keep his commands, because this is the whole of being human" (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Scholars debate whether one hand or two wrote these verses; the rabbis said the book was kept in Scripture because it ends with words of Torah (Bavli Shabbat 30b).

In the book's last chapters hevel is tied to time. Life itself is "your vapor of a life" and "all your days of vapor" (Ecclesiastes 9:9); "All that comes is vapor" (Ecclesiastes 11:8); "boyhood and black hair are vapor" (Ecclesiastes 11:10). Here the sense of a breath that passes is strongest, and it gives urgency to the call to joy. The final cry, "Vapor of vapors" (Ecclesiastes 12:8), comes straight after the picture of death, as the breath goes back to God (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

sections.h: "The dead do not know a thing" (Ecclesiastes 9)
sections.b: Ecclesiastes 9:5–6 and 9:10 are the Old Testament's bluntest words about the dead: they know nothing, have no wages and no share, and in Sheol "there is no doing and no reckoning, no knowledge and no wisdom". Most scholars read them as the older Israelite picture of Sheol as silence (Psalm 6:5; Psalm 115:17). Jewish tradition read them of this world or morally of the wicked (Bavli Berakhot 18a–b). Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant teachers read them as death seen from under the sun; Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses read them as plain teaching that the dead are unconscious. The verses also bear on whether the dead know of the living and whether the living may pray for them.

"With a good heart drink your wine, for what you do has already pleased God" (Ecclesiastes 9:7). Qohelet ranks wine among the daily gifts God approves, as Psalm 104:15 praises "wine that makes people glad at heart". He also knows its misuse: woe to the land whose princes feast at daybreak, happy the land whose princes eat "to be strong and not to be drunk" (Ecclesiastes 10:16–17), and "wine makes life glad" (Ecclesiastes 10:19) is said with an edge.

sections.h: "See life with a woman you love" (Ecclesiastes 9:9)
sections.b: In the middle of his call to joy Qohelet names married love as part of a person's "share in life" (Ecclesiastes 9:9). The advice matches Siduri's in Gilgamesh, who tells the hero to let his wife delight in his embrace, and the counsel of Proverbs 5:18 to rejoice in the wife of one's youth. It stands in tension with Qohelet's harsh words about women in Ecclesiastes 7:26–28, and readers weigh the two passages differently.

"Whatever is in your power to do, do it with your strength" (Ecclesiastes 9:10): because Sheol ends all work, work now. Chapter 10 adds that skill saves effort ("wisdom's gain is that it brings success", Ecclesiastes 10:10) and that laziness lets the house drip (Ecclesiastes 10:18). Chapter 11 tells the hearer to sow morning and evening without waiting for certainty (Ecclesiastes 11:4–6). Monastic readers heard the book as contempt of the world; Luther heard it as a charter for daily work in one's calling.

"Wisdom is better than might" and "better than weapons of battle", Qohelet says, but "a poor man's wisdom is looked down on" and "one sinner can wreck a great deal of good" (Ecclesiastes 9:16–18). A little folly spoils it like dead flies in perfume (Ecclesiastes 10:1). Wisdom is real but fragile.

The book ends where Proverbs and Job place the root of wisdom: "Fear God and keep his commands" (Ecclesiastes 12:13; compare Proverbs 1:7; Job 28:28). "Fear God" is Qohelet's own phrase (Ecclesiastes 5:7); "keep his commands" is the language of Deuteronomy.

sections.b: Ecclesiastes 10 advises those who serve rulers: stay calm when the ruler is angry (Ecclesiastes 10:4), expect mistakes from those in power (Ecclesiastes 10:5–7), and never curse the king, "for a bird of the sky will carry off the sound" (Ecclesiastes 10:20). "Woe to you, land! Your king is a lad" (Ecclesiastes 10:16), but happy the land whose king is "a son of free men" (Ecclesiastes 10:17). A great king who besieges a small town is defeated by a poor man's wisdom (Ecclesiastes 9:14–15).

"Words from a wise mouth are grace, but a fool's own lips gulp him down" (Ecclesiastes 10:12, compare Proverbs 18:7). The fool "piles up words" (Ecclesiastes 10:14), and even a private curse will be reported (Ecclesiastes 10:20). The rabbis read the snake that bites when no spell has been whispered (Ecclesiastes 10:11) as a picture of the slanderer (Bavli Arakhin 15b).

sections.h: "Send your bread out over the surface of the water" (Ecclesiastes 11:1–2)
sections.b: The Targum, Rashi and many Christian preachers read Ecclesiastes 11:1–2 as a call to give: send your bread to the needy and "give a share to seven, and even to eight", and it will come back after many days. Others read the verses as advice on trade or risk. The Egyptian Instruction of Ankhsheshonq has a close parallel about a good deed thrown into the river.

God is "the God who makes everything", whose work no one can know, any more than how bones take shape in the womb (Ecclesiastes 11:5). The young are told, "Remember your Creator in the days of your prime" (Ecclesiastes 12:1), and the poem ends by reversing Genesis 2:7: "the dust goes back to the earth as it was, and the spirit goes back to God, who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

sections.h: The house of forever and the mourners (Ecclesiastes 12:5)
sections.b: "The human is on his way to his house of forever, and the mourners circle about in the street" (Ecclesiastes 12:5). "House of forever" for the tomb is found in Egyptian, Phoenician and later Jewish inscriptions. The mourners are likely professional mourners, whom the Mishnah required even at a poor man's funeral (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4; compare Jeremiah 9:17–18).

sections.h: "Beyond these" and the end of the book (Ecclesiastes 12:12–14)
sections.b: The epilogue warns against anything beyond "these" words, since "making many books has no end" (Ecclesiastes 12:12), and it closes with the fear of God and the commands (Ecclesiastes 12:13). The rabbis said the sages had wanted to withdraw the book because its words contradict one another, but kept it because it begins and ends with words of Torah (Bavli Shabbat 30b). Many scholars, following Sheppard, see Ecclesiastes 12:13–14 as a conclusion that reads the book in the light of the Torah.

Ecclesiastes 9:5–10 knows no hope beyond death, and Ecclesiastes 12:7 says only that the spirit goes back to God. Christian readers have set these verses beside Daniel 12:2 and the New Testament, reading Qohelet as an honest account of death seen from under the sun, which the resurrection answers (1 Corinthians 15:32, quoting Isaiah 22:13).

"Time and chance meet them all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11): the swift do not always win, and people are caught like fish in a net by "an evil time" (Ecclesiastes 9:12). Qohelet does not deny God's rule ("in God's hand", Ecclesiastes 9:1), but insists that no one can read it from events or know "what God does" (Ecclesiastes 11:5).

Ecclesiastes 9:7–9 closely matches Siduri's advice to Gilgamesh in the Old Babylonian epic: eat, be merry, wear clean clothes, wash, delight in wife and child. The world upside down of Ecclesiastes 10:5–7 recalls the Egyptian Admonitions of Ipuwer, Ecclesiastes 11:1 the Instruction of Ankhsheshonq, and the portrait of old age in Ecclesiastes 12 the lament on age in the Instruction of Ptahhotep.
